summary: Defines three MIME content types for carrying EDI (electronic data interchange) business documents in email, since there are many EDI specifications. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: EDI is a set of formats that companies use to exchange orders and invoices in a fixed, machine-readable shape. This document says how to put such a document into an email message: by labelling the message part with the right content type, one of three depending on which EDI standard the document follows.

subtitle: How to carry electronic data interchange documents as MIME body parts, using three content types.

tldr.problem: Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) is a way for trading partners to exchange structured transactions, and email is the natural way to carry them, but MIME had no agreed way to label an EDI document.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three MIME content types: Application/EDIFACT, Application/EDI-X12 and Application/EDI-consent, each with no required parameters and an optional CHARSET parameter, and each carried with a transfer encoding when the data is not printable text.
tldr.outcome: Formatted business documents can travel in ordinary email. The specification changes nothing about the EDI documents themselves and provides no security of its own.

facts.label: Required parameters
facts.value: None, for all three content types

facts.label: MIME version in the sample message

today: RFC 1767 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1995, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document itself states that it provides no security mechanisms of its own, so it is meant to be used together with whatever protection the trading partners need.

sections.title: What the Specification Does
sections.content:
Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) provides a means of conducting structured transactions between trading partners. The delivery mechanism for these types of transactions in a paper world has been the postal system, so it is to be expected that electronic mail would serve as a natural delivery mechanism for electronic transactions. This specification permits formatted electronic business interchanges to be encapsulated within MIME messages.

For the specification effort, the basic building block from EDI is an interchange. The specification pertains only to the encapsulation of EDI objects within the MIME environment. It intends no changes in those objects from the primary specifications that define the syntax and semantics of them. EDI transactions take place through a variety of carriage and exchange mechanisms, and this specification adds to that repertoire by permitting convenient carriage through Internet email.

Since there are many different EDI specifications, the document defines three distinct categories as three different MIME content types. One is Application/EDI-X12, indicating that the contents conform to the range of specifications developed through the X12 standards organization. Another is Application/EDIFACT, indicating that the contents conform to the range of specifications developed by the United Nations Working Party 4 Group of Experts 1 EDIFACT boards. The last category covers all other specifications, and is Application/EDI-consent.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not change how EDI documents are written. It only says how to label one when it is carried as an email attachment, and it does that with three labels, because there are many EDI standards and a receiver needs to know which family the document belongs to.

sections.title: The Three Content Types
sections.content:
The three content types all share the same shape: the MIME type name is Application, there are no required parameters, and the only optional parameter is CHARSET as defined for MIME. The encoding considerations for all three are that they may need BASE64 or QUOTED-PRINTABLE transfer encoding, and the security considerations point to the separate section of the document.

Application/EDIFACT contains data as specified for electronic data interchange by the EDIFACT specifications. It is a generic mechanism for sending any EDIFACT interchange, and the object is self-defining in terms of indicating which specific EDI objects are included. The rationale given is that the EDIFACT specifications are accepted standards for a class of inter-organization transactions, and this permits their transmission over the Internet via email.

Application/EDI-X12 contains data as specified for electronic data interchange by the ASC X12 specifications. It is a generic mechanism for sending any ASC X12 interchange, again self-defining. The rationale is the same: the ASC X12 EDI specifications are accepted standards for a class of inter-organization transactions, and this permits their transmission over the Internet via email.

Application/EDI-consent contains data as specified for electronic data interchange with the consent of an explicit, bilateral trading partner agreement exchanging the EDI-consent traffic. Use of EDI-consent only provides a standard mechanism for wrapping the EDI objects, and does not specify any of the details about those objects. The rationale is that existing practice for exchanging EDI includes a very wide range of specifications that are not part of the usual accredited standards world; nevertheless, this traffic is substantial and well-established, and the content type provides a means of delimiting such content in a standard fashion. X12 and EDIFACT objects must be sent using their assigned MIME content type. EDI-consent is for all other EDI objects, but only according to trading partner agreements between the originator and the recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of the three labels name a specific EDI standard family, and the third is a catch-all for everything else. The catch-all is only for documents the two partners have agreed between themselves to exchange in that way.

sections.title: Why a Transfer Encoding May Be Needed
sections.content:
The document gives the same encoding note for each of the three content types. Most EDI data is textual, but special characters such as some delimiters may be non-printable ASCII, or some data may be pure binary. For EDI objects containing such data, the MIME transfer mechanism may need to encode the object in Content-Transfer-Encoding:quoted-printable or base64.

This is the same mechanism MIME uses for any other body part that is not safe to put in a mail message as plain text: the content is transformed into a printable form for transport, and the Content-Transfer-Encoding header says which transformation was used so that the receiver can undo it.
sections.plainLanguage: Most EDI text is fine to put straight into an email, but some delimiters are not printable characters, and some payloads are binary. When that happens, MIME's usual transfer encoding carries it, and the header records which encoding was used.

sections.title: A Sample Message
sections.content: The document gives one example, an EDIFACT interchange sent as a MIME message, to show the gist of the formatting required. The headers are the ordinary mail headers, followed by Mime-Version: 1.0, a Content-Type naming the content type, a Content-Transfer-Encoding, and then the interchange itself in the body.
sections.plainLanguage: A single EDI interchange in an email needs no more than the normal mail headers, the MIME version, the content type that says which EDI standard the body follows, and a line saying how the body was encoded for transport.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EDI transactions typically include sensitive data, so transmission often needs to attend to authentication, data integrity, privacy, access control and non-repudiation concerns. This specification permits transmission of such sensitive data via Internet mail and other services that support MIME object encapsulation. For transmission of sensitive data, it is essential that appropriate security services, such as authentication, privacy and/or non-repudiation be provided.

The specification does not itself provide any security-related mechanisms. As needed and appropriate, such mechanisms MUST be added, either via Internet MIME-based security services or any other services that are appropriate to the user requirements, such as those provided by EDI-based standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Orders and invoices are business secrets, so this document carries no protection of its own. Whatever security the two trading partners need has to be added on top, either with the security services MIME offers or with whatever their own EDI standards provide.

sections.title: How the Message Reaches the Other Side
sections.content:
The appendix is written for readers who know EDI but not Internet electronic mail. Internet electronic mail follows the classic user agent and mail transfer agent model, in which user software produces a standardized object which is transferred via standard exchange protocols. An Internet electronic mail object comprises a collection of headers, followed by a possibly structured body. The headers specify information such as author and recipient addresses, subject summary, creation date and handling node names, and are defined by RFC 822 and RFC 1123. If the body is structured, it conforms to the rules of MIME. A structured body may have parts encoded in different text character sets, or even of entirely different types of data, such as voice or graphics.

The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol performs the primary task of message transmission. User posting and delivery interactions between the user agent and the message transfer agent on the same machine are not standardized and are platform-specific.

An EDI-related use of Internet MIME email has, at least, the components shown in the document: a business program or database, an EDI translator, MIME encapsulation, RFC 822 packaging, mail submission, SMTP relaying, mail delivery, RFC 822 and MIME stripping, another EDI translator, and business processing. The first and last lines show components normal to all EDI activities, so it is only the EDI transmission components that are replaced with Internet modules.
sections.plainLanguage: An EDI document still has to be turned into an EDI document at each end; the email carries it in between. The document shows the chain of steps from the business system on the sender's side to the business system on the receiver's side.

viz.caption: THE THREE CONTENT TYPES AND THEIR PARAMETERS
THE SAMPLE MESSAGE FROM RFC 1767 SECTION 5

data.title: A single EDIFACT interchange
data.code:
To:  <<recipient organization EDI email address>>
Subject:
From: <<sending organization EDI email address>>
Date:
Mime-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: Application/EDIFACT
Content-Transfer-Encoding:  QUOTED-PRINTABLE

<<standard EDIFACT Interchange goes here>>

viz.caption: THE COMPONENTS OF AN EDI MESSAGE OVER EMAIL (RFC 1767 APPENDIX)

data.title: Component chain
data.code:
Business Program/Data base -> EDI Translator ->
-> MIME encapsulation -> RFC822 packaging -> mail
submission ->
-> SMTP relaying ->
-> mail delivery -> RFC822 & Mime stripping ->
-> EDI Translator -> Business processing
